analysis.one_liner: Gives patients the right to see and correct their own medical records and bans selling them without consent.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 1999 with sponsors from both parties, the bill was referred to three House committees and then three subcommittees, and it never received a House vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Every time you see a doctor, fill a prescription, or file an insurance claim, a record is created. This bill would have set federal rules for who could see, use, or sell that record. Patients would gain the right to inspect and copy their own health information, ask for corrections, and be told how their data is handled. Health information could not be sold or commercially published, disclosures for lawsuits or police work would require a judge's sign-off, and violators would face fines, prison, and exclusion from Medicare, Medicaid, and the federal employees' health program.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a medical record: patients would get enforceable control over who reads, uses, or sells their health information, and people harmed by an unauthorized disclosure could sue.

how_it_helps.text: Patients could inspect and copy their own health records within 45 days of asking, and could request corrections, with denial reasons and dispute statements attached to the record going forward.

The bill prohibited disclosing individually identifiable health information without a written, signed authorization, and banned selling or commercially publishing it, with fraud used to obtain records facing up to $250,000 in fines and 10 years in prison.
Disclosures for civil lawsuits and criminal law enforcement would need a subpoena plus a court order finding the need for the information clearly outweighed each patient's privacy interest.

Victims of knowing or negligent violations could sue for court relief with attorney's fees available, and entities that substantially failed to comply could be barred from Medicare, Medicaid, and the federal employees' health program.

Doctors, insurers, employers, and schools holding health data would have to safeguard it, limit access to staff who need it, sign binding agreements with contractors, and post clear notices of their confidentiality practices.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, life insurers, employers, schools, and health care providers, which would bear the cost of building safeguards, compliance policies, and contractor agreements, and would lose their ability to freely use, disclose, or sell patient records for marketing, underwriting, and other secondary purposes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and health data holders

drawbacks.text: The bill let record-holders charge patients reasonable fees to inspect and copy their own files, which could deter people from exercising the new right.

The private right of action offered only equitable relief, not money damages, so an individual harmed by a disclosure could get a court order but no direct compensation unless the criminal or exclusion penalties applied.

It would preempt state privacy laws that cover the same ground, potentially displacing stronger protections some states had already adopted, though carve-outs preserved state rules on mental health, communicable disease, abuse reporting, and minors.

The bill applied to schools, universities, and employers of two or more workers, a broad reach that would impose compliance costs across many kinds of organizations, and the sponsors themselves built in an annual study of the law's effect on the quality of health research, acknowledging the tension between privacy rules and research access.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the privacy gains were real and the bill was thoughtfully built: it preserved treatment, payment, and public-health disclosures, created a supervised path for researchers to use archived data, and layered penalties from fines to program exclusion. The honest costs are the compliance burden on every organization holding health records and the possibility that the fee-for-access and no-damages features made patient rights harder to use than they looked. But the question was settled by inaction, not by this weighing: the bill never advanced far enough to be amended or debated.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House subcommittees from July 1999 until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, never reaching a committee vote or the House floor.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Shays of Connecticut introduced the bill on July 1, 1999, joined by Representatives Hilliard, LaTourette, and McHugh.
The House referred it to three committees at once: Commerce, Ways and Means, and Government Reform.

By late July 1999 it had been sent to the Commerce health subcommittee, the Government Reform subcommittee on management and information technology, and the Commerce subcommittee on health and environment.
No further action was taken on the bill for the rest of the 106th Congress, which ended January 3, 2001.
The bill carried four subject areas in the record and would have preempted most state laws covering the same matters, making it a sweeping federal privacy framework rather than a narrow fix.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations that hold and profit from health data: insurers, employers, marketers, and other data users kept operating under no comprehensive federal privacy law for medical records, since Congress never acted on this bill or on competing privacy proposals in the 106th Congress.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor the day it was introduced.

for.name: Reps. Hilliard, LaTourette, and McHugh
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Received the bill as the committee of primary referral in July 1999; it was sent to a health subcommittee and no markup or floor action ever followed.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer and Rep. Dan Burton

against.what_they_did: Their committees received secondary referrals of the bill in July 1999; neither took it up before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start, with two Republicans and two Democrats cosponsoring, but the bill died in committee without any roll-call vote, so there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from selling or commercially publishing patient records and required written authorization for most disclosures, cutting off a lucrative secondary use of medical data. Patients' privacy and insurers' freedom to trade in that data pull in opposite directions.

Employers of two or more workers were covered by the bill and would have faced limits on how employee health information could be used, disclosed, or inspected, restricting a practice they had handled without federal rules.

Providers would have gained a clear federal rulebook and good-faith protections for authorized disclosures, but borne compliance costs and faced exclusion from Medicare, Medicaid, and the federal employees' health program for substantial failures.

Companies that encode, manage, or analyze health data, and anyone who profited from reselling it, would have been bound by written compliance agreements and the sale ban, closing the market in personal medical records.

Unapproved research disclosures would have been prohibited, but the bill created a structured pathway for researchers to access archived records, including tissue and blood banks, under board review and written agreements, giving researchers a reliable legal basis they previously lacked.
